title: East Flank Podcast #10 Eastern Flank citizens: Ready for a crisis?
content:
In the latest episode of the EastFlank Podcast, journalists from newsrooms across the EU and NATO’s eastern flank take a closer look at civil defence in a region living next door to Russia’s war against Ukraine.

As Russia intensifies its hybrid activities, preparedness is becoming an increasingly urgent issue. We compare warning systems, emergency alerts and shelter networks across countries on the eastern flank and ask a simple question: how prepared are governments – and their citizens – for a real crisis?
As always, the discussion builds on our latest collaborative report, produced by journalists from across the region – this time focusing on civil defence and emergency preparedness.

Listen to the latest episode of the EastFlank Podcast.

title: Civil Defence on the EU and NATO’s Eastern Flank [INFOGRAPHIC]
content:
The infographic highlights the key elements of civilian preparedness for emergencies – from the recommended period of self-sufficiency and essential supplies to emergency power sources and public warning systems.

One of the most common recommendations is to be prepared to remain self-sufficient for at least 72 hours. However, approaches vary from country to country. Latvia recommends preparing for 3–7 days, while Slovakia advises being prepared for up to 14 days in the event of a prolonged power outage. Bulgaria and Hungary do not specify a single nationwide recommended timeframe.

title: 72 Hours or Two Weeks? Europe Takes Different Approaches to How Prepared People Should Be for a Crisis
content:
This raises the same practical question across Europe: how long should an individual household be able to cope on its own?

Some countries already have a clear answer – at least 72 hours. Others recommend being prepared for three to seven days, or even two weeks in certain scenarios. In some countries, there is no general preparedness timeframe at all.

The differences are not limited to the number of days. Countries also have different ideas about what preparedness actually means: in some, it means having water, food and medicines at home; elsewhere, it also includes alternative heating, cooking, electricity and communication, as well as access to civil protection infrastructure.

Three days have become something of a symbol of civil preparedness in Europe in recent years.

title: EU countries tackle fuel prices on their own, but calls are growing for joint EU action
content:
Robert Fico is lashing out at the EU instead of cutting taxes or taxing Slovnaft, but he is not the only one calling for a coordinated response.

Fuel prices are rising again as a result of the US war against Iran, the latest conflict to erupt in the Middle East in its wake, and the ongoing Russian war against Ukraine. Several EU member states are trying to cushion the impact with a range of measures.

On Tuesday, Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico criticised the European Union, saying that while it has no influence over the military conflicts affecting oil prices, it continues to finance Ukraine, which is at war with Russia. According to Fico, the EU is leaving its member states exposed to the consequences of the oil crisis while expecting them “to compensate for astronomical fuel prices at the expense of pensions, healthcare or education”.

The Slovak prime minister is calling for an extraordinary EU summit to seek a European-level solution to bring fuel prices down. He has also urged the countries of the Visegrád Four to work together.

title: The Middle Corridor could make Bulgaria strategic for NATO’s Eastern Flank too
content:
Europe’s geopolitical map is no longer being redrawn only on the battlefield. While NATO builds more resilient infrastructure along its Eastern Flank, the EU is looking for new routes to Asia to reduce its dependence on the trade corridors that have run through Russia until now. This is precisely where Bulgaria could prove to be far more than a country on the periphery of the Old Continent.

But what do the Middle Corridor and the Alliance’s military mobility have in common? The route linking China and Central Asia with Europe – across the Caspian Sea and the Caucasus, and from there via Turkey and the Black Sea to the European transport network – is expected to carry ever larger volumes of goods. At the same time, the roads, railways, bridges and ports along the Eastern Flank must be able to ensure the rapid movement and resupply of troops and equipment in the event of a crisis.

title: AI Sites Posing as News Outlets Spread to Finland
content:
Websites created and maintained entirely by artificial intelligence are becoming more common, and even the news media are not immune to this phenomenon. Over the past year, a number of websites resembling news outlets have appeared in Finland, such as UKK Uutiset and The Intelligent, whose content is entirely generated by artificial intelligence.

These sites publish content sourced from the websites of the leading daily Helsingin Sanomat, the public media service Yle and the tabloid press, as well as from social media. Occasionally, the authors are characters created by artificial intelligence who pose as journalists. On The Intelligent, AI journalists even publish opinion pieces.

Faktabaari reviewed Finnish AI news websites and found that these two sites, which react to daily current affairs, regularly highlight far-right themes. Based on social media, their reach is not extensive, but the sites may offer indications of future developments.

title: Whistleblower protection in Romania: A legal framework still struggling in practice
content:
The law protects whistleblowers from retaliation, allows them to report wrongdoing through internal and external channels, and designates the National Integrity Agency (ANI) as the central authority for external reporting. Yet the number of reports remains low, with significant differences between institutions.

The main challenge is no longer the absence of a legal framework, but the gap between the protections established by law and how the system actually works in practice, according to several comparative studies and analyses.

Romania had a whistleblower protection mechanism as early as 2004. But it applied only to public-sector employees and did not provide official reporting channels or protection mechanisms considered adequate.

A major overhaul came in 2022 with the adoption of Law No. 361/2022 on the protection of whistleblowers in the public interest. The new legislation established a more comprehensive reporting system and made the National Integrity Agency (ANI) the main authority responsible for external reports.

title: EU migration policy tightens. Frontex and return hubs take centre stage
content:
The Munich Migration Meeting was originally conceived as a gathering of Germany and its neighbouring countries. German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt said the meeting had since become “a genuine platform for discussing migration”, with participants agreeing that “we want to push forward the shift in migration policy”.

Magnus Brunner, the European Commissioner for Internal Affairs and Migration, highlighted what he described as clear progress: “Irregular migration has fallen by 55 per cent over the past two years, and by more than another third this year.” In his view, this shows that Europe has managed to “put its house in order” through a series of reforms.

“This is the result of a consistent policy over the past two years, and the new rules have yet to reach their full effect,” the Commissioner said. He pointed to Germany as a country playing a leading role. “Europe needs a strong Germany,” he added, particularly in the fight against irregular migration.

title: Is Poland’s National Evacuation Plan Really a Plan to Displace Poles?
content:
The complex geopolitical situation and the ongoing war on NATO’s eastern border require countries in the region to constantly review their security procedures. But as national crisis-management plans are updated, a parallel phenomenon is emerging online: organised disinformation designed to undermine the public’s sense of security and stability. In recent days, a familiar narrative has resurfaced, claiming that government rescue and evacuation plans are in fact a covert project to displace citizens.

The threat in Poland’s immediate neighbourhood is not a matter of conspiracy theories, but a reality reflected in daily intelligence reports. Russia continues to test NATO’s boundaries. Last week, within the space of just 24 hours, NATO defence systems had to respond to a drone shot down over Lithuania and an incident in which a Russian frigate fired flares at a Danish helicopter. At the same time, suspicious acts of sabotage disrupted rail traffic in the Netherlands.

title: Poland Pushes to Slow EU ETS Reform and Ease Climate Rules
content:
After years of tightening EU climate policy, the European Commission is proposing changes that would ease some of the rules of the Emissions Trading System. On 17 July 2026, the Commission presented its proposal for a post-2030 revision of the EU ETS. In several areas, it would reduce short-term pressure on industry, but it does not mean abandoning the EU’s climate targets or dismantling the system.

The ETS revision, now being fast-tracked through the European Parliament, is intended to give some breathing room to European industries struggling with competition from China. But Brussels remains divided over the pace at which emission allowances should be reduced, how the market should operate and what should happen to modernisation funds.

Poland is campaigning hard for a significant easing of the emissions trading rules. Together with a group of ten Central and Eastern European countries, Warsaw is pushing for deeper concessions and greater solidarity between EU member states. Donald Tusk’s government argues that excessively high CO2 allowance prices threaten household budgets, industrial competitiveness and Poland’s energy security.

title: Who are Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman: And why does the EU sanctions decision matter?
content:
The European Union has extended sanctions against more than 3,000 individuals and entities linked to Russia for another three years. At the same time, two Russian billionaires – Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman – have been removed from the EU sanctions list.

EU member states agreed to extend the restrictive measures until 22 September 2029. The sanctions include travel restrictions, asset freezes and a ban on making funds or other economic resources available to sanctioned individuals and entities. The European Council says the measures are intended to target those responsible for undermining or threatening Ukraine’s territorial integrity, sovereignty and independence.

Until now, the EU’s individual sanctions related to Russia’s war against Ukraine had generally been renewed every six months. This time, member states opted for a significantly longer extension, providing greater predictability about the future of the restrictions.

title: Poland and Hungary Win the race for EU recovery funds – but only just
content:
The Recovery and Resilience Facility (RRF), the main component of the EU’s €800-billion-plus NextGenerationEU recovery package, is now entering its final phase. Member states had until August 30 to submit their final payment requests, together with evidence that the agreed reforms and investments had been completed. The European Commission has until December 31 to make the remaining payments.

Poland was among the countries facing the greatest delays in accessing the funds. For years, Brussels withheld payments under the EU’s rule-of-law conditionality mechanism, amid a dispute over judicial independence under the previous Law and Justice (PiS) government.

That left Poland with considerably less time to deliver on its commitments — and created a race to complete the programme before the EU funding window closed.

The Recovery and Resilience Facility played a key role in mitigating the economic and social impact of the COVID-19 pandemic while preparing the EU for long-term development.

title: EC pledges to strengthen member states’ response to security threats
content:
Particular attention should be paid to plans for a new EU security strategy, including proposals for a Security Council and an EU alert mechanism to respond to security threats that do not reach the level of armed aggression. Critics have previously warned that such a move could risk overlapping with NATO security mechanisms.

With the war in Ukraine increasingly affecting Europe’s eastern flank and Russia stepping up its sabotage attacks and drone campaigns, security and defence became the main theme of the European Commission president’s annual address.

This week alone, Poland raised the alarm after Russia struck a train travelling from Kyiv to Warsaw. At the time of the attack, the train was at the Yahodyn railway station, approximately two kilometres from the Ukrainian-Polish border. Shortly afterwards, Prime Minister Donald Tusk warned that such escalations were increasingly approaching the borders of European countries: “The coming weeks and months are expected to be a very intense period in Russia’s activities.”

title: Did the EU force Google to remove hotel prices from its search engine?
content:
On the 9th of September, an anonymous account on the social network X published a post about changes made by Google to its search engine in Europe. The post is partly true, but supplements the facts with unfounded conclusions about EU requirements and Google’s motives, implying that changes making the popular search engine less convenient for Europeans were introduced as a result of decisions made in Brussels.

On the 8th of September, Google did indeed introduce changes to search results in the European Union. They affect, for example, how search results for hotels, airlines, and restaurants are displayed. In some European countries, certain sections of the service no longer show features that were previously available, such as real-time prices. Most of the changes are linked to decisions adopted by the European Commission (EC) in July concerning Google’s compliance with the Digital Markets Act.

The EC imposed two fines on Google totalling 890 million euros. A 460 million euros fine was imposed because Google gave preference in its search results to its own services, such as Google Flights and Google Hotels, over competing services.

title: Has Russia deployed 80,000 troops near the Latvian and Estonian borders?
content:
Talk of possible mobilisation in Russia, together with reports that the aggressor state is preparing up to 20,000 beds in civilian hospitals near the Baltic Sea, has added to public concern. But public anxiety also creates fertile ground for false information.

In early September, a social media post claimed that Russia had deployed a “new army” of up to 80,000 troops near its borders with Latvia and Estonia, citing purported information from Lithuanian intelligence. The claim is false.

On 1 September this year, an anonymous account called “Кассандра” (Kassandra) published a post on Threads with an alarming introduction: “Don’t make any plans for autumn. We’re taking the Baltics. Lithuanian intelligence reports that the Baltic people are soon going to be ***.” The post claimed that Russian armed forces had moved hundreds of military trucks to the borders with Latvia and Estonia, that new offensive divisions had been formed from brigades stationed there, and that the total strength of this “new army” was between 50,000 and 80,000 troops.

The post also claimed that “fresh satellite images confirm the troop buildup. The concentration of equipment is alarming NATO and the Baltic people.”

title: The Bank of Latvia has not “printed” new money since 2014. Was Prime Minister Kulbergs wrong?
content:
In the discussion, it was pointed out that “price increases are the direct responsibility of The Bank of Latvia (Latvijas Banka, LB)”. When it was suggested that it “continually “prints” new money”, Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs (United List) replied that the central bank “has not printed money since we joined the eurozone in 2014”. The discussion was joined not only by other users but also by LB, which pointed out that it both “issues euro banknotes and coins and participates in their printing”.

LB’s post on X about money issuance and its involvement in “printing”, as well as the charts it provided, sparked a new thread, with the bank being accused of lying. “Here, the Bank of Latvia is lying. The causes of current inflation are not only the situation in the Middle East or what is happening in Russia, but also monetary policy, specifically the ECB’s interest-rate increases, as well as government policy, spending more than it earns and borrowing even more.”

title: Will Canada become part of Europe? What von der Leyen’s initiative means for security
content:
Although Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney praised von der Leyen’s move when addressing the European Parliament the following day, diplomats speaking behind the scenes say they had not been warned and do not really understand what the status of an “associated member state” would actually mean. Closer ties with Canada are particularly important for Latvia, as Canada has been a leading NATO country deploying troops here to deter Russian aggression since 2014.

Foreign policy researcher Mārtiņš Vargulis says the new “association” could most easily be put into practice in the areas of security and defence production. Meanwhile, Latvia’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs told Delfi that it supports deeper ties with Canada, particularly in the field of security, but that in order to formulate a specific Latvian position on the “association”, it is necessary to wait until the terms of such an arrangement are defined in greater detail.

title: The EU considers ChatGPT a search engine. But strict rules may miss its most important part
content:
ChatGPT has now been placed in the same regulatory category as Google and Bing in the European Union. At the end of August, the European Commission designated it as a so-called Very Large Online Search Engine (VLOSE). For OpenAI, this means an additional layer of obligations under the Digital Services Act (DSA).

The decision is primarily linked to ChatGPT’s web-search capabilities. The Commission considers ChatGPT a “hybrid” service: the chatbot answers users’ questions and can search the internet for information while doing so. Under the DSA, its search function therefore falls under the definition of an online search engine.

OpenAI reported an average of 159.1 million monthly active users in the EU over the six months to March 2026. That is more than three times the 45-million-user threshold above which the Commission can designate a service as a VLOSE.

Following the designation, OpenAI has four months to comply with the new rules. The additional obligations for VLOSEs should therefore apply to ChatGPT by January 2027 at the latest.

Among other things, OpenAI will have to monitor its algorithms more closely and better document and account for how sources are selected.

title: One year in prison for unsolicited “dick pic”: Czechia moves to implement EU law on violence against women
content:
Sending an unsolicited photograph of someone’s genitals – commonly known as a “dick pic” – could become punishable by up to one year in prison in Czechia. The measure is part of the country’s implementation of the EU directive on combating violence against women and domestic violence.

The directive entered into force in June 2024 and EU member states must transpose it into national law by mid-June 2027.

In recent weeks, Czechia has opened a public consultation on how to implement the directive. The Ministry of Justice has presented an initial draft law that would make the unsolicited sending of so-called dick pics – photographs of male genitalia – a criminal offence. The legislation would also cover photographs of female genitalia.

Those found guilty could face up to one year in prison.

Under the ministry’s proposal, criminal liability would depend on whether the behaviour could cause serious harm and whether the sender was aware of that possibility.
